name: Dry needling / acupuncture

lead: Dry needling inserts a thin needle into tight muscle knots, called trigger points, to ease pain. People try it on neck and upper-back muscles that they connect to rounded or hunched posture, and sometimes on the jaw.

The chain is tight muscles needled, less tension in the neck and shoulders, then easier upright posture. Systematic reviews describe short-term pain benefit in some conditions, from small studies with methodological limits. No study examines how posture looks afterward.

paras: A trained clinician inserts needles into specific muscle points for a short period in a session, often as a series alongside stretching or exercise. It overlaps with acupuncture, though the professions dispute how they relate.

Soreness and bruising are common. Rare serious events such as pneumothorax or infection are reported, so it is done by trained clinicians; practitioner scope of practice is disputed in several US states.

chain: Less tension in neck and shoulders
angle.text: People try needling of neck and upper-back trigger points to loosen tight muscles that they connect to rounded or hunched posture. The path runs from needled muscles to less tension to easier upright posture. Short-term pain relief has some support in studies; effects on how posture looks have not been studied.

lead: Dry needling is a technique in which a thin solid needle is inserted into muscle, most often at myofascial trigger points, to treat muscle pain. It is distinct in theory from acupuncture, though the two use similar needles and the relationship is disputed between professions [1][2].

In looksmaxxing and posture discussions it is mentioned as a way to release tight muscles in the neck, jaw and shoulders. It is a clinical pain-management technique and is not an established appearance treatment.
Systematic reviews describe short-term pain benefits in some conditions but note small, low-quality studies and methodological flaws, and the evidence for long-term benefit is limited [1][3][4].

paras: A filiform needle is inserted into skin and muscle without injecting any substance, in contrast with wet needling that uses a local anesthetic or other agent. Clinicians often aim to elicit a local twitch response, a brief involuntary contraction of the muscle band [1][2].

Czech physician Karel Lewit described deep dry needling for trigger points in 1979, and Janet Travell and David Simons' 1983 trigger point manual is credited with the term [1][2]. A 1994 study of upper trapezius trigger points compared lidocaine injection with dry needling and emphasized the importance of eliciting a local twitch response [5].

Acupuncture practitioners often regard dry needling as an adaptation of acupuncture, and in 2011 a US acupuncture accreditation body described it that way. Many physical therapists and chiropractors describe it as a biomedical procedure based on anatomy and trigger point theory rather than traditional Chinese medicine concepts. Several authors have reported substantial overlap between trigger points and acupuncture points [2].
No studies found examining dry needling for appearance outcomes such as posture-related facial or neck appearance. Studies of pain conditions exist.

A 2001 systematic review examined needling therapies for myofascial trigger point pain [6]. A 2013 meta-analysis of upper-quarter myofascial pain reported short-term pain reduction while urging caution because of study flaws [2][7]. A Cochrane review of acupuncture and dry needling for low back pain was updated in 2005 [8]. A 2014 literature review discussed implications for clinical practice guidelines [3]. Wikipedia summarizes later reviews as finding insufficient high-quality evidence for pain and disability outcomes, and low-quality studies in low back pain [2].

Common effects are soreness lasting a day or two and bruising [1]. Rarer serious events reported include pneumothorax, nerve or spinal injury and infection, and in one large self-reported survey 8.6% of respondents reported at least one adverse effect [2].

The US FDA regulates the needle as a device, not who may use it. Scope-of-practice disputes between physical therapists, chiropractors and acupuncturists have reached state boards and courts, and in 2016 the American Medical Association called for training standards [2].
